lessonTitle: Interstitial Lung Disease and Lung Cancer: Restriction, Gas Transfer and the Lung Mass

blocks.text: A 63-year-old retired bricklayer who smoked for 40 years has been coughing for three months and brought up streaks of blood twice this week. Separately, his brother, a non-smoker, has a dry cough and breathlessness on walking and crackles at both lung bases that sound like Velcro being pulled apart. One brother has a lung that cannot expand because it is scarred; the other has a lung where an abnormal clone of cells is growing.

blocks.markdown: **Interstitial lung disease (ILD)** is a group of disorders that inflame or scar the **interstitium**, the tissue between the alveolar epithelium and the capillary endothelium. Fibrosis stiffens the lung (lowering compliance), so the lungs cannot fully inflate: this is a **restrictive** defect. The thickened alveolar wall and loss of capillary bed also impair gas exchange. The prototype is **idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF)**, a progressive scarring disease with the histological pattern of usual interstitial pneumonia, with subpleural, basal-predominant fibrosis and honeycombing. Other causes include occupational dust (asbestos, silica), drugs, connective tissue disease and hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

### Spirometry and gas transfer in restriction

In restriction, both FEV1 and FVC fall, but the **FEV1/FVC ratio is normal or high** (above about 0.70) because airflow is not obstructed; the stiff lung recoils briskly. Lung volumes show a reduced **total lung capacity (TLC)**. Reduced **gas transfer** is measured by the diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLCO, also called transfer factor, TLCO), expressed as a percentage of the predicted value for age, sex and height. In interstitial disease it falls because the alveolar-capillary membrane is thickened and the surface area for gas exchange is reduced.

rows: Reduced in emphysema; normal in asthma

blocks.title: Reading a restrictive pattern
blocks.prompt: A patient has FEV1 1.7 L, FVC 2.0 L, predicted FVC 4.0 L, and DLCO 40% of predicted. Interpret.

steps.text: FEV1/FVC = 1.7 / 2.0 = 0.85, which is above 0.70, so there is no obstruction.
FVC as a percentage of predicted = 2.0 / 4.0 = 50%, which is markedly reduced.

A reduced FVC with a normal or high ratio indicates a restrictive pattern. The low DLCO points to loss or thickening of the alveolar-capillary membrane, as in interstitial fibrosis, rather than a purely extrapulmonary cause of restriction such as obesity or neuromuscular weakness, in which gas transfer is typically preserved.

blocks.answer: Restrictive pattern with reduced gas transfer, consistent with interstitial lung disease.

blocks.markdown:
### Lung cancer: histological types

Smoking causes most lung cancers, with risk related to total exposure measured in **pack-years** (packs smoked per day multiplied by years smoked, where a pack is 20 cigarettes). Cancers are classified as **small cell lung cancer (SCLC)** or **non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC)**, and NSCLC divides mainly into squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma and large cell carcinoma.

blocks.caption: A standard measure of cumulative smoking exposure.

rows: Keratin pearls and intercellular bridges; may cavitate; PTHrP causing hypercalcaemia
Glandular, mucin-producing; commonest type overall and in never-smokers; EGFR mutations in some
Associated, but also occurs in never-smokers
Small cells with scant cytoplasm, neuroendocrine; early metastasis; ectopic ADH or ACTH
Very strong; almost all patients are smokers
Undifferentiated large cells; diagnosis of exclusion
blocks.caption: Main histological types of lung cancer

blocks.title: Quantifying smoking exposure
blocks.prompt: A man smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 25 years. Calculate pack-years and say why this matters.

steps.text: Cigarettes per day divided by 20 gives packs per day: 20 / 20 = 1 pack per day.
Risk of lung cancer and COPD rises with cumulative dose, so pack-years help to estimate risk and decide on investigation.

blocks.markdown:
### Imaging of a lung mass

Chest radiography is often the first test. A **solitary pulmonary nodule** is a discrete opacity up to 3 cm, and a **mass** is larger than 3 cm. Features favouring malignancy include a size over 3 cm, **spiculated or irregular margins**, **cavitation with a thick, irregular wall** (especially squamous carcinoma), enlargement of the **hilum** (lymph nodes), **lobar collapse** (bronchial obstruction), **pleural effusion** and rib destruction. A smooth, well-defined outline and dense central or laminated calcification favour a benign lesion. CT then characterises the lesion and stages the disease, and tissue biopsy confirms the diagnosis.

items: Spiculated edge: tumour growing along septa, suggests malignancy.
Cavitation with a thick irregular wall: squamous carcinoma or abscess.
Lobar collapse: endobronchial tumour obstructing a bronchus.
Pleural effusion: pleural involvement, a sign of advanced disease.

blocks.title: Two different problems on the same film
blocks.text: Interstitial lung disease gives diffuse, reticular opacities with small lung volumes, whereas a tumour gives a focal mass. Always correlate imaging with spirometry: a restrictive lung function pattern with reduced DLCO points to the interstitium, not to a mass.

points: ILD stiffens the lung through interstitial fibrosis, giving a restrictive spirometry pattern with reduced FVC, a normal or high FEV1/FVC ratio, reduced TLC and reduced gas transfer.
Lung cancer includes squamous cell carcinoma and small cell carcinoma, which are central and very strongly smoking-related, and adenocarcinoma, which is peripheral and also occurs in never-smokers.
On chest radiography a spiculated, cavitating mass with hilar enlargement, collapse or effusion suggests malignancy and needs CT and tissue diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has FEV1 2.1 L, FVC 2.5 L (55% of predicted) and FEV1/FVC 0.84. Which pattern is this?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a reduced FVC with a normal or raised FEV1/FVC ratio is restrictive.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: obstruction has a low ratio, below about 0.70.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: the FVC is only 55% of predicted.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: the ratio is not reduced, so there is no obstructive component.

questions.explanation: The ratio of 0.84 excludes obstruction, while the FVC at 55% of predicted shows that the lungs cannot fully inflate. This combination defines a restrictive pattern.

questions.stem: Why is the diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) reduced in pulmonary fibrosis?

options.text: Thickened alveolar-capillary membrane and loss of surface area impair gas diffusion
Increased lung compliance causes air trapping

questions.correctOptionText: Thickened alveolar-capillary membrane and loss of surface area impair gas diffusion

distractorRationale.a: Correct: fibrosis thickens the diffusion barrier and destroys capillary bed.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: airway narrowing is the mechanism of obstruction, not of reduced gas transfer in fibrosis.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: compliance is reduced, not increased, in fibrosis.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: muscle weakness causes restriction with normal gas transfer.

questions.explanation: Gas must cross the alveolar-capillary membrane, and fibrosis thickens this barrier while destroying capillaries. DLCO therefore falls, in contrast to extrapulmonary causes of restriction in which the lung parenchyma is normal.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old heavy smoker has a centrally placed lung tumour that cavitates, and his serum calcium is raised because of PTHrP secretion. Which histological type is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: central, cavitating, keratinising tumours that secrete PTHrP are squamous carcinomas.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: small cell carcinoma is central but secretes ADH or ACTH and rarely cavitates.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: hamartoma is a benign, popcorn-calcified peripheral nodule.

questions.explanation: Squamous carcinoma arises in central bronchi in response to smoking, and may produce keratin and cavitate. Secretion of parathyroid hormone-related peptide explains the hypercalcaemia.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman who has never smoked has a 2 cm peripheral nodule on chest radiography, and biopsy shows glandular, mucin-producing cells. Which diagnosis is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: adenocarcinoma is peripheral, glandular and the commonest type in never-smokers.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: squamous carcinoma is central, keratinising and very strongly linked to smoking.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: small cell carcinoma is almost exclusively in smokers and is neuroendocrine.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: large cell carcinoma is undifferentiated and lacks glandular features.

questions.explanation: Glandular architecture with mucin secretion is the definition of adenocarcinoma, and its peripheral location and occurrence in non-smokers are typical. It is the commonest lung cancer overall.

questions.stem: On a chest radiograph, which finding in a solitary lung nodule most strongly suggests malignancy?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: spiculation reflects tumour extension along septa and is a malignant feature.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: dense central or laminated calcification suggests a benign lesion such as a granuloma.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: smooth margins favour a benign lesion.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: stability over two years is reassuring and favours benign disease.

questions.explanation: Irregular or spiculated margins reflect invasive growth, so they raise suspicion of cancer. Benign features include smooth outline, certain patterns of calcification and long-term stability.

questions.stem: A man has smoked 15 cigarettes a day for 40 years. Using 1 pack = 20 cigarettes, calculate his smoking exposure in pack-years.
questions.explanation: Fifteen cigarettes per day is 0.75 packs per day, and 0.75 x 40 years = 30 pack-years. Cumulative exposure helps to assess his risk of lung cancer.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected interstitial lung disease has a measured DLCO of 14.4 mmol/min/kPa and a predicted value of 24.0 mmol/min/kPa. Express the measured value as a percentage of predicted.
questions.explanation: The percentage of predicted is 14.4 / 24.0 x 100 = 60%. This is below the usual lower limit of normal (about 80%), indicating reduced gas transfer consistent with interstitial disease.

questions.stem: Describe the spirometric and gas transfer findings in interstitial lung disease and explain them in terms of the underlying pathology.
markingGuide: Interstitial fibrosis reduces lung compliance so lungs cannot fully inflate
FEV1/FVC normal or high, as there is no airway obstruction
DLCO reduced because of thickened alveolar-capillary membrane and loss of capillary bed
Examples of causes or features: IPF with basal Velcro crackles and clubbing
questions.explanation: A stiff, scarred lung is restricted in volume and its gas exchange surface is damaged. This produces the restrictive pattern with a low transfer factor.

questions.stem: Name the four main histological types of lung cancer, describing the usual location, one distinguishing pathological or clinical feature and the association with smoking for each of squamous, adenocarcinoma and small cell types.
markingGuide: Types: squamous cell, adenocarcinoma, small cell, large cell
Squamous: central, keratinisation, may cavitate, PTHrP hypercalcaemia, very strongly smoking-related
Adenocarcinoma: peripheral, glandular and mucin-producing, commonest in never-smokers, associated but not exclusive to smoking
Small cell: central, neuroendocrine, ectopic ADH or ACTH, early metastasis, almost exclusively in smokers
Large cell as undifferentiated, diagnosis of exclusion
questions.explanation: The histological type predicts location, behaviour and paraneoplastic syndromes. Smoking is linked to all types but is strongest for squamous and small cell carcinoma.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old smoker has a chest radiograph showing a 4 cm mass in the right upper zone with an irregular, spiculated edge and an enlarged right hilum. Describe the radiographic features that suggest malignancy, list other findings that indicate local spread, and state how the diagnosis is confirmed.
markingGuide: Size above 3 cm defines a mass and raises concern
Spiculated or irregular margins suggest malignancy
Cavitation with thick irregular wall can occur in squamous carcinoma
Other features: lobar collapse, pleural effusion, rib destruction
Diagnosis: CT for characterisation and staging, then tissue biopsy for histology
questions.explanation: Imaging features reflect how the tumour grows: it invades along septa, obstructs bronchi and spreads to nodes and pleura. A radiograph raises suspicion, but only tissue confirms the type.
